{"docket_number": "83-5424", "additional_docket_numbers": null, "term": "1984", "first_party": "Glen Burton Ake", "first_party_label": "Petitioner", "second_party": "Oklahoma", "second_party_label": "Respondent", "manner_of_jurisdiction": "Writ of certiorari", "lower_court": "Oklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals", "argued": ["1984-11-07T06:00:00Z"], "question": "

In capital cases, does the Fourteenth Amendment require the government to provide an indigent defendant with the psychiatric assistance necessary to prepare an effective insanity defense?

", "facts_of_the_case": "

In 1979, Glen Burton Ake was arrested and charged with murder for killing a couple in Oklahoma. At trial, his behavior was so abnormal that the court ordered a prolonged mental examination to determine his competency to stand trial. After six months of examination, a state psychiatrist declared Ake unfit for trial and in need of a “maximum security facility.” Six weeks after this declaration, the same psychiatrist found that, when Ake was on his anti-psychotic medication, he was stable and competent to stand trial; the state resumed proceedings.

Ake intended to assert the insanity defense, so a psychiatrist had to determine Ake’s mental state at the time of the killings. Because Ake could not afford to hire a psychiatrist, his attorney requested that the state provide him one. The court refused and rejected Ake’s argument that the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment required the government to provide indigent defendants with a psychiatrist to allow them to raise a meaningful insanity defense. Without a psychiatrist, Ake was unable to provide any evidence as to his mental state at the time of the offense. Absent this evidence, jurors were instructed that Ake was to be presumed sane at the time of the offense. The jury subsequently rejected Ake’s insanity defense and convicted him on all counts. At the sentencing hearing, Ake—still unable to afford a psychiatrist—could not provide expert testimony to mitigate his offense and was sentenced to death. Ake appealed to the Oklahoma Criminal Court of Appeals, which affirmed and held that the government was not responsible for providing psychiatric help to indigent defendants charged with capital crimes.

", "conclusion": "

Yes. Justice Thurgood Marshall wrote the opinion for the 8-1 majority. The Court held that, when a defendant has made a preliminary showing that his sanity at the time of the offense will be at issue during the trial, the Constitution requires the government to provide psychiatric assistance if the defendant cannot afford it. The Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment requires state-provided assistance in cases where there is a private interest that will be affected by the state’s actions, value that will be derived from the additional safeguards, and when providing the assistance will only be a minimal burden to the state. All three of these factors were present in this case. Furthermore, both justice and the Fourteenth Amendment require a defendant to be able to participate meaningfully in the judicial proceedings, which is impossible if the government were to deny this type of assistance to Ake and similar defendants.

Chief Justice Warren E. Burger wrote a concurring opinion in which he noted that the Court’s decision applies only to capital cases.

Justice William H. Rehnquist wrote a dissenting opinion in which he, like Justice Burger, argued that this decision should apply only to capital cases. Furthermore, he argued that this rule should provide for an independent psychiatric evaluation, not a comprehensive defense consultant.

analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "Your arguments next in Ake against Oklahoma. She's a girlfriend called New Orleans. She lost this one. She probably had a few possible jobs. I'm afraid she won't. She's just kind of argumentative. I'm afraid she'll be back. I feel child about 90 for his main argument. Yes, 70 for his rep. Mr. Spitzer. Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the court. In this case, the state of Oklahoma convicted an indigent defendant of murder, having refused his request for expert psychiatric or psychological assistance that was necessary for him to make any real defense to the charges against him. Additionally, the state requested and obtained the death penalty based in part on an expert prediction of the defendant's future dangerousness that the defendant was unable to rebut because he could not afford the same expert assistance. And the state tried this defendant in the face of obvious and recognized indications that he may not have been competent to stand trial. We submit that the Constitution, as a matter of due process, equal protection, and the right to effective assistance of counsel, requires the states to provide indigent defendants with such necessary assistance. In October of 1979... To just assert it to every case or to capital cases or to just the sentencing part of the capital case, do you break it down at all? Well, Your Honor, what's before the court, of course, is a capital case, and the court need not decide more than is before it. But to the extent, which I think is a large extent, that these questions go to the accuracy of the truth-finding process at the trial, I think the logic would apply them to other cases as well as capital cases. With respect to the sentencing proceeding, of course, a capital sentencing proceeding is a considerably different procedure than a sentencing proceeding in a normal case, and there different considerations might well apply. In other words, you might say that even if it is not applicable to criminal charges generally, that it must be in a capital case. I would certainly say that, Your Honor. And as I will explain in more detail later, to the extent that this court applies a due process balancing test, as it did in Libel against Streeter, then it's legitimate to consider the state's countervailing interest in fiscal economy balanced against the interest of the defendant. And, of course, the interest of the defendant is greater in a capital case than it is in other kinds of cases. And so those considerations may legitimately be considered. In October 1979... Mr. Spitzer, do you plan to address the jurisdictional problem during your argument today? Your Honor, I'll address it right now. The state argues that Mr. Ake waived his right to bring these issues to this court by not including them in a motion for new trial in the trial court. There are two answers to that. The first is the State Court of Criminal Appeals dealt with these issues on the merits, and under this court's jurisprudence, that's all that's required to preserve the issue. Well, it didn't really deal with a due process argument, did it, on the merits? Your Honor, I think both arguments were made to it, that the court's treatment of these arguments... I couldn't find anything in the opinion that indicated that it dealt with a due process argument. Well, certainly the court's treatment in its opinion was brief, but in the briefs that were presented to the Court of Criminal Appeals, those arguments were made. And I think the court dealt with the issue, and I think it's a constitutional issue that's important. The second argument, the second response, though, Your Honor, is that it would have been absolutely futile to raise this in a motion for a new trial. The point of a motion for a new trial is to give the trial judge a chance to correct his errors at that point, to hold a new trial right away without going through an appellate process if he recognizes the error of what has happened. But in this case, the trial court committed no error under the law of Oklahoma. The trial court was correctly following the law of Oklahoma in denying these experts, and bringing it to his attention was pointless because he couldn't have given that. But that's not an exception under Oklahoma law, I assume, for failing to bring the motion for a new trial on that ground? I don't know whether it is under Oklahoma law, Your Honor. You've researched the cases, though, in Oklahoma? As to whether futility is an exception on that point, I don't know the answer under Oklahoma law. And have you found any case suggesting that it would be? No, Your Honor. No, Your Honor. But I think it's a consideration that this court can legitimately apply. There's really no point in requiring counsel to exercise a pointless procedure. And you don't think that there is an adequate and independent state grounds, then, existing here? I believe not, Your Honor. And I believe that because the Oklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals did address the merits of this issue, it's properly in this court. Mr. Spitzer, you don't cite, in support of the argument you just made, Douglas in Alabama in 380 U.S. Are you familiar with it? Your Honor, I'm afraid I'm not familiar with it. Well, I thought, in that case, we held on something like futility ground, that there, to the extent that the Alabama rule, that was Alabama, requires objection after each and every question in this plunge, it is plainly inadequate to borrow a review of the federal question presented, holding that whether or not it was an inadequate state grounds or review was a question for us to decide. I would have supposed you to rely on it. I thought that decision seems to foreclose any argument that was an inadequate state grounds. That's a different argument than you present. You say that your submission is just because the Court of Criminal Appeals addressed the merits that there is jurisdiction here. Now, suppose the Court of Criminal Appeals says we think that there was an objection, that there should have been an objection at trial, or there should have been a motion for a new trial on this ground. There was not. So, it is barred. We cannot reach it. But in the event the Supreme Court of the United States thinks that this is not an adequate state ground, we're going to address the merits. And they go ahead and address the merits. Now, you wouldn't think that their addressing the merits would then give us jurisdiction, do you? Well, Your Honor, I don't think that's what happened. I can see that there would be a question that would survive, the one that Justice Brennan refers to as to whether that really is an adequate or an independent state ground. But that isn't your submission. Well, that question would certainly survive, and I'm glad to adopt Justice Brennan's position on that question. I think you would. But that's not what happened here. The Court first addressed the issue on the merits and then said, by the way, it was not raised in the motion for a new trial. And I think— But it's still alternate grounds. Still completely alternate grounds. And if a state court decides a question before it where there's a claim constitutional violation on both state and federal constitutional grounds, making clear that they're both separate ones, we say that is an adequate state ground even though the federal constitutional issue is discussed at length. Well, Your Honor, I think I've cited a couple of cases in my briefs where the Court has ruled that when the state did treat the federal question on the merits, that was all that was necessary. But not if they give also a statement that we're also deciding this case on state constitutional grounds. Your Honor, I guess I just don't think the state's decision was that clear in giving an alternate state ground. I do think this issue was plainly presented to the trial court, and the trial court could not have done other than it did under Oklahoma law. And I believe the issue then was adequately preserved. Mr. Bitzer, do you think Michigan against Long has any bearing on this issue? Your Honor, I must confess I am not familiar with what that case held on this point either. Well, then I guess you wouldn't be able to enlighten me on the question. I'm afraid not. Your Honor, assuming that this court has jurisdiction, if I may pass to the merits of the case, Mr. Ake was arrested some six weeks after the killings and he confessed at that time that he had committed the act. While he was in jail and at his arraignment about 11 weeks later, his conduct was so bizarre that the trial judge, on his own motion, had him examined by a psychiatrist and sent to the state mental hospital for observation, but only on the issue of competency to stand trial. The hospital concluded after a month that he was not competent, and at a hearing the psychiatrist testified that he was paranoid schizophrenic, that he had extreme delusions, that he lived in a different dimension, that he did not accept the ordinary concepts of right and wrong. Between the alleged murder and the competency examination? The murder was in October, Your Honor, and the competency examination, the first one was in February. The defense counsel had raised the issue, at least to a certain extent, at the preliminary hearing in January. That's the first hearing of which we have any transcript. And he asked questions to the sheriff's deputies about whether they had observed Ake having fits and seizures at the jail and asked questions of witnesses about Ake's mental state at the time of the crime, but there was no formal proceeding directed to competency until the pretrial, until the arraignment in February. After this finding of no competence, Ake was recommitted to the hospital, but again, for care and treatment, not for any observation with respect to sanity at the time of the crime. Six weeks later, the hospital reported that on medication he had improved to the point where he was competent, and he was sent back for trial. No hearing was held to determine whether he was competent at that time. At this point, his counsel moved for funds to retain a psychiatrist to examine him with respect to his mental condition at the time of the crime and to assist in preparing and presenting the defense of insanity. Mr. The proposition that the court could designate the psychiatrist? Your Honor, that's correct, as an alternative. He requested first funds to retain a psychiatrist, but as an alternative, as a fallback, he suggested that the defense would be content if the court would appoint a neutral court psychiatrist. Both requests were denied, and both on the same ground, and it was not denied because the trial judge had any doubt that sanity was an issue or that such assistance would be very useful to the defendant. It was denied simply on the ground that under Oklahoma law, no such assistance of either kind could be provided in any case. As a result of that decision, there was no expert testimony at Ake's trial with respect to his mental condition at the time of the crime, no direct testimony. In an attempt to present an insanity defense, defense counsel, who were court appointed, called the three doctors who examined Ake with respect to his competence. They all testified that he was mentally ill, diagnosed as a paranoid schizophrenic. Two of them specifically mentioned that they were relying on the criteria in the American Psychiatric Association's Diagnostic Manual, and those criteria require at least a six-month duration of symptoms for such a diagnosis. Both psychiatrists testified that the illness might have been affecting his conduct, might have been apparent, was the words that one used, on the day of the crime. Dr. Garcia, specifically in answer to a hypothetical question, testified that someone with Ake's condition, who had consumed drugs and alcohol, which he had at the day of the crime, might not have been able to know right from wrong under that circumstance. But on course examination, each doctor was pressed and each doctor admitted that he could form no professional opinion and could give no expert testimony about Ake's mental condition at the time of the crime, because he had not performed an examination with that in view. The jury was then charged, in accordance with Oklahoma law, that the defendant had the burden of proof of raising a reasonable doubt as to sanity. And because the state appears to dispute that, I'd like to read very briefly from the charge to the jury. It's in the joint appendix of 57 and 58, and I'm omitting unnecessary words. The law presumes every person to be sane and able to distinguish right from wrong, as applied to any particular act, until a reasonable doubt of his sanity is raised by competent evidence. When the plea of insanity is interposed, the burden of proof is on the defendant to introduce sufficient evidence to raise in the minds of the jury a reasonable doubt of the defendant's sanity at the time of the commission of the acts in question. When this is done, the burden of proof is on the state to prove the sanity of the defendant by competent evidence beyond a reasonable doubt. In closing argument, the prosecutor argued that the defendant had not met his burden of raising a reasonable doubt, and the reason he gave was that no psychiatrist had so testified. The prosecutor didn't argue that there was an absence of late. Excuse me, Your Honor. Point in your petition for certiorari. Yes, Your Honor, I believe we did. The prosecutor argued that because there was no expert testimony, no doubt had been raised. Excuse me, Your Honor. Of course, the reason why there was no expert testimony was because the defendant had been denied the psychiatric examination. Maybe I didn't make my question clear. Did you present the question of the court's instruction? Oh, no, Your Honor, and there's nothing wrong with the court's instruction under Oklahoma law, and I do not contend that Oklahoma cannot require the defendant to shoulder the initial burden of raising a reasonable doubt about his sanity at the time of the crime. Not at all. That was a proper instruction. What was improper was a violation of due process, was the catch-22, if I may use that phrase, of requiring the defendant to shoulder that burden, and then depriving him of what was effectively the only means of doing so, of shouldering that burden. The jury found the defendant guilty, and the Court of Criminal Appeals, in affirming, relied on the same reasoning. They affirmed not on the ground that the state had proved its burden of showing sanity beyond a reasonable doubt, but on the ground that the defendant had never raised a reasonable doubt about sanity. And again, the only evidence they pointed to was the lack of psychiatric opinion testimony, the testimony the defendant was unable to obtain because of his poverty. It was, at least in your main brief, Davis against the United States, an 1897 case, which was that, which held that as soon as there is any indication of any mental factor in a case, the burden of proof shifts. Well, Your Honor, as I understand it, that was a rule for the federal courts and not necessarily a rule for the state courts. But Oklahoma, I think, follows that rule, or at least Oklahoma's position is that when the defendant raises a reasonable doubt by sufficient evidence, the burden shifts. But the holding of the Oklahoma Court here was that the burden had never shifted, was that it was the defendant who hadn't satisfied his burden, and therefore the defendant is the party in this case who had the burden throughout the case. It never shifted. We believe that under those circumstances, with the burden on the defendant, with, as a practical matter, that burden, carryable only with expert testimony, the defendant had a right to that expert assistance. The state concedes in this court that there are circumstances where such expert testimony is necessary to a fair trial and would therefore be required by the Constitution. We submit that this is such a case. Insanity is not a subject where the observation of lay witnesses or the common sense reasoning of lay jurors is sufficient. Only a trained clinician can recognize the often puzzling symptoms of mental disease, can explain to a jury the etiology of the disease and how it may affect someone's conduct. Mr. Spitzer, may I ask you a question here? Would it have been, at least theoretically possible, that you might have called lay witnesses, friends, relatives, and the like, who knew your client at the period when the crime was committed, who could have testified to whatever behavior they knew about? And then you might have asked one of these three psychiatrists on hypothetical questions, and based on the following assumptions, which would be supported by the lay testimony, what would your opinion be? Would there be any question? Couldn't you possibly have crossed the threshold in that manner? Your Honor, that is a theoretical possibility, but I think it's not more than theoretical, certainly in a case like this. The ability of a lay witness to recognize and to report symptoms of mental illness may be present in some cases where the symptoms are floret, where the illness is obvious. But that is certainly not always the case and may well not have been the case here. Oregon, I cited in my brief several cases, and there's a long line of cases, I'm sorry, in Oklahoma, where lay testimony such as that is held not even to raise a reasonable doubt. In Garrett against State, for example, the defendant was an 80-year-old woman who shot a foster child of hers. She'd raised a dozen foster children, shot one one day, and two other people. One of the victims testified that she looked crazy, she looked bizarre when she was doing it. The defendant testified on the stand that she couldn't remember anything about what happened. The Oklahoma court held, never raised a reasonable doubt. In high against State, two deputy sheriffs who were the jailers testified that the defendant did not appear to them to be a normal person, that he had no memory, that he was unintelligible, that he was grossly lacking in personal hygiene, held no reasonable doubt of sanity ever raised. In Oklahoma, is there some overt time when the burden shifts? Your Honor, I understand that under current Oklahoma practice, which has changed since this trial, the judge does not instruct the jury on insanity until the judge determines that it's an issue in the case. And at that point, the judge instructs only that the state has the burden of proving beyond a reasonable doubt. But at this time, that was not the practice, and the judge simply instructed his jury on both and allowed the jury to determine that. Just so I get the extent of your position clearer, suppose under the present Oklahoma practice, the judge says a reasonable doubt about sanity's bed and raisins, so the state has the burden. And the state then puts on some testimony. Is it part of your submission here that you, even in those circumstances, would have the right to have your own psychiatrist appointed? I think the answer is yes, but the reasoning is different. And in those circumstances, it may be that the defendant needs psychiatric assistance in order to rebut or cross-examine the state's psychiatrist, just as the state has been held in most circuits to have a right to do the same. Or you want a psychiatrist who may testify quite contrary to the other psychiatrist. Exactly so. I think in this case, the answer is the same, but for different reasons. In this case, the defendant apparently needed that assistance not to rebut the state's case, but to shoulder his burden. But I think the result in either of those cases is the same. Mr. Spitzer, is it your position that the psychiatrist must be selected by counsel for the defendant? Not necessarily, Your Honor. I think that the state could have the same flexibility as it does in providing lawyers for indigent defendants. There could be a panel from which a person could be appointed. Could the court simply appoint? The court, I think, could appoint one. I think the key thing is that once appointed, the psychiatrist must be there to assist and consult with defense counsel as well as to examine the defendant. It's not, in other words, the state's doctor. It is the defense's doctor. Not a neutral psychiatrist, but one who, in effect, would participate in assisting the defense counsel in conducting a trial. That is our primary submission, Justice Powell. But let me say that even if the court were to conclude that all that the Constitution requires is some psychiatric examination where a defendant's mental condition is an issue, as occurred, for example, in United States, Israel Smith against Baldy, even that was not done here, and even that would require reversal in this case. Why would it require? It wasn't requested here, was it? Your Honor, I think the defense request at the pretrial conference can be interpreted to include that, that what the defense was asking was for some psychiatric examination. Well, certainly the point raised, at least in the opinion of the Oklahoma Court of Criminal Appeals, simply says he's entitled to be furnished a psychiatrist. That's the way the Oklahoma—I mean, I don't think you really preserve, unless the idea that the greater includes the lesser, which I don't think our cases hold. Well, I think in a case like this, the greater certainly includes the lesser. At the pretrial hearing where the request was made, defense counsel phrased the request in a variety of different ways, but I think it was clear to the trial judge that what they were asking at a minimum was that there be some psychiatric examination of this defendant with respect to his sanity at the time of the crime. Well, you think it was made equally clear to the Oklahoma Court of Appeals? Your Honor, I would have to look at the brief that was filed there, but certainly United States against—X-Rell Smith against Baldy was repeatedly cited by the trial court, had been relied upon by the Oklahoma Court in the case which it cited in this case. And so I think that question was one that the court would have understood to be before even if it was not explicitly before in so many words. I have little time, and let me briefly touch on the other two issues that we've raised in this case. The first is, at the sentencing hearing, Ake was again disadvantaged severely by the lack of this same expert assistance. The psychiatrist predicted his future dangerousness, and I should mention they were called as defense witnesses at the merits phase of the trial, but the prosecution had previously announced its intention to call those as its own witnesses. And so I think the fact that the testimony came out earlier is not of great significance. But that— But would you—you're not submitting that—you're not submitting that the defendant has a right to a—a convicted defendant has a right to a psychiatrist in every single capital sentencing? No, Your Honor, that's not our— It's only where there's this element of future dangerousness that the jury has to find. Those are the facts in this case, Your Honor, and that's what our argument is directed to here. Well, how much broader do you think it is than that? I really don't know that, Your Honor. I think, though, that here the need is clearer by a wide margin because there is no effective rebuttal to expert opinion testimony except expert opinion testimony or—and perhaps the ability to cross-examine with the assistance of an expert to help you cross-examine. Was cross-examination of the state's witnesses on the question of future dangerousness conducted at the sentencing proceeding? No, Your Honor. These witnesses were not called at the sentencing proceeding. They testified— I guess that could have been done by the defendant himself on the question of future dangerousness. Your Honor, certainly the defendant could have tried to cross-examine on this question, but we don't require lawyers to be educated about the internal disputes among the psychiatric profession, about their ability to make this kind of prediction without any expert either to testify on his behalf or to assist him in that kind of cross-examination. I think it was more than we could reasonably expect for defense counsel to do that. You say that you really can't expect a lawyer to be able to cross-examine an expert witness without an expert witness of his own to suggest questions? That's certainly not always true, Your Honor. It depends, I think, on the nature of the expertise and the nature of the case. Certainly, if one were to read Justice Blackmun's dissent in our barefoot decision, there's a good deal of psychological literature, psychiatric literature available on the issue. That's true, Your Honor. And I'm not saying that that's not a theoretical possibility. But we have a situation here. Oklahoma pays defense counsel a very modest sum to defend a first-degree murder case and provides them with none of the same assistance that it provides the state in these same kinds of cases. Oklahoma makes funds available, makes experts available for the state. I think the real answer to the question is that the defendant was entitled to expert assistance to rebut by expert opinion testimony these opinions if that was possible. But such an expert could also be of great assistance in helping defense counsel to know how to cross-examine. Our final point had to do with the defendant's competency to stand trial. He was receiving a large amount of Thorazine during his trial and acting in a way that certainly raised questions about his competence. And I can't say I know he was incompetent, but I don't think the courts of Oklahoma are in a position to say that they know he was competent. Under this court's precedence, and paid against Robinson and drove against Missouri, we submit it was the court's duty when the court was aware and acknowledged those questions to inquire into the subject. If I may, I'd like to reserve what remains of my time for rebuttal. We'll resume there at 1 o'clock, Mr. Attorney General. Mr. Attorney General. Mr. Chief Justice, may it please the court. On October 15, 1979, the petitioner in this case, Glenn Burton Ake, committed the murder of Reverend Richard Douglas and his wife Marilyn. And it wasn't until some eight months later at trial that the issue we're here on today was ever even raised. And when it was finally raised, a right to a psychiatric examination, be it constitutional or otherwise, I expect that's the issue we're here to decide, it was raised just a few days before trial in an oral motion. And the attorney at that point in time saw fit to bring no one forward, nobody that had seen the defendant, if you will, on the date of the crime, not his father, not his grandfather, who had helped him move furniture the morning of the date of the crime. He brought no one forward to supplement his motion. Mr. Attorney General. I thought that before the trial commenced that he had been committed for observation. It is correct. To make sure that he was competent to stand trial. Mr. Justice. Is that right? Oh, no, that's exactly correct. I was about to draw the distinction between the issue of sanity at the time of the crime and competency at the time of trial. Oh, I think that's, but you don't, you must be saying at least that just because there was an issue about competency to stand trial, that doesn't necessarily mean that there was ever an issue about competency at the time of the crime or insanity at the time of the trial. Exactly, and we get a little bit confused in Oklahoma with the interchangeability of those two terms. At the time of this trial, it was sanity at the time of the crime as well as the issue of sanity at the time of trial. Now in Oklahoma, the law has changed, and we talk about competency to stand trial, as this court, of course, has in past cases, and sanity at the time of the crime. There is a whole body of case law, of course, that says to plead not guilty by reason of insanity does not automatically put competency at the time of trial into issue. And, of course, we believe the reverse is true. Some several months, four or five months after the crime, you do have the issue of competency raised. But we don't believe that automatically calls into issue sanity at the time of the crime. There are two different tests, two different times, frankly, two different people. Well, General Turpin, what if the competency inquiry for trial purposes develops testimony by the state psychiatrist that the defendant suffers from a chronic mental condition that at least could have existed at the time of the commission of the offense? Does that, in and of itself, raise additional concerns that would make it appropriate or necessary for the court to consider appointment of some psychiatric expert for the defense? I think we have to look at a test, if you will, and I'm not sure one exists except by looking at Grope versus Missouri, where they do say you've got to look at three different factors. I say they say. I mean you say. This court said that you look at, number one, prior medical opinion. Number two, the history of irrational behavior. And number three, the demeanor at trial. Now, that's for competency at trial, of course. I think that same test could be applied to sanity at the time of the crime for determining the nature or quantum of type of evidence we look at to decide this very test. In our case, there was no prior medical opinion. He'd never been adjudicated or committed before. In our case, there was no history of irrational behavior. In fact, the only history was his mother testified that he had a normal childhood. There is something that you brought up where Dr. William Allen said that we do have a history of him talking with Jesus at the age of seven after his daddy beat him for cigarettes, for smoking cigarettes. I'll suggest to you that's a subjective symptom, if you will. That's what the petitioner told this doctor. Otherwise, there's nothing in the record except for the fact that mother said personally that he had a very normal childhood. That's in the record. So you've got an objective observation there versus a subjective symptom. Well, I don't believe you've answered my question yet. Well, I'm trying to. And I think I'd suggest that I don't think it does automatically. To answer your question most directly, I don't think it does automatically trigger the right to further psychiatric examination in and of itself just based on that competency issue.
